analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from using non-compete agreements against hourly and lower-wage workers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee without a hearing or a vote; no other action was taken during the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal labor law to void every existing non-compete agreement and bar employers from enforcing or writing new ones for most hourly and lower-wage workers (the "non-exempt" employees covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act, such as shift workers, retail and food-service staff, and many office workers). Non-competes prevent workers from taking a job with a competing company, starting a similar business, or working in an area—often for years after they leave a job. The bill would let those workers change jobs freely, which research generally links to higher wages, while carving out an explicit protection for employers to keep employees from sharing trade secrets.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly and lower-wage workers currently bound by non-competes would be freed to take jobs with competitors, work in their field, or start similar businesses without legal threat. Research on state bans suggests workers who gain mobility see wage increases, since employers must compete to keep them. Because the bill reaches every non-exempt employee, tens of millions of workers would gain the legal right to switch employers.

how_it_helps.text: It voids any non-compete agreement already in place and prohibits employers from enforcing or threatening to enforce one against covered workers.
It bans employers from entering into, extending, or renewing new non-competes going forward, covering agreements that restrict work for another employer, work in a geographic area, or similar work.
Violations become enforceable under the Fair Labor Standards Act, allowing workers to sue for legal or equitable relief rather than depending on a government agency.
It does not limit employers' ability to require workers not to share trade secrets.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use non-competes to retain hourly and lower-wage staff would lose that tool, potentially facing more turnover and higher training and recruiting costs, which they might pass on through prices or reduced investment.

drawbacks.text: Some employers argue non-competes protect investments in training and client relationships; this bill would eliminate that tool for hourly and lower-wage workers, though it explicitly preserves the ability to require employees not to share trade secrets.
The ban's reach is broad: it voids existing agreements and bars new ones for all non-exempt workers, going further than rules that would restrict non-competes only above a wage threshold.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—wage growth and job mobility for tens of millions of hourly workers—is large and well documented in economic research on states that have banned non-competes. The drawbacks are real but modest: employers lose a tool for protecting client relationships and training investments, though the bill preserves trade-secret protections for genuinely confidential information, which addresses the most serious objection. On balance, the benefit to ordinary workers outweighs the cost to employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate labor committee, which never took it up, so it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The only actions ever taken were its introduction on February 9, 2023, and its referral the same day to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it to the full Senate, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill expired and would have had to be reintroduced to move forward.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use non-competes to restrict hourly and lower-wage workers kept that power, which is widely associated with holding down wages and job mobility.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that use non-competes on low-wage workers

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to bar non-competes for non-exempt workers.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Joined Rubio in introducing the bill.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral—no hearing, no markup, no vote—letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican led the bill with one Democratic cosponsor, but the committee never considered it, so no party-line vote ever took place.

industries.industry: Employers that use non-competes for hourly and lower-wage staff
industries.note: Franchise chains, staffing firms, service companies, and manufacturers that routinely have low-wage workers sign non-competes would lose the ability to enforce or renew them, increasing turnover but freeing workers to take better jobs.
The bill explicitly preserves agreements barring disclosure of trade secrets, so firms whose main concern is confidential information keep that protection.
Companies trying to hire workers bound by non-competes would gain access to a larger pool of candidates.
